q: Which Europe-wide balancing platform pools the opposite imbalances of the participating TSOs without ranking energy bids on common merit order lists?
answer: The platform for the imbalance netting process: it consists of the imbalance netting process function and the TSO-TSO settlement function and applies a multilateral TSO-TSO model (no activation optimisation function and no common merit order lists, which the replacement-reserve and frequency-restoration platforms use) (Article 22(2)).

q: For which of the Europe-wide balancing energy exchange platforms is the implementation-framework proposal drafted only by the TSOs that run the reserve replacement process, instead of by all TSOs?
answer: The platform for balancing energy from replacement reserves: its proposal is developed by all TSOs performing the reserve replacement process pursuant to Part IV of Regulation (EU) 2017/1485 (Article 19(1)); for the manual-activation, automatic-activation and netting platforms it is all TSOs.

q: Eighteen months after approval of a platform's implementation framework, TSOs may propose changes to it. For which Europe-wide energy exchange platform may that change proposal also reopen the platform's basic principles (common governance, multilateral TSO-TSO model, common merit order lists), not just the implementation framework?
answer: The platform for balancing energy from frequency restoration reserves with automatic activation: its amendment proposal is made “pursuant to paragraph 1 and of the principles set in paragraph 2” (Article 21(5)). The corresponding paragraph for the manual-activation platform (Article 20(5)) mentions only paragraph 1.

q: How may frequency restoration power be interchanged between load-frequency control areas of one synchronous area when the reserve activation is manual rather than automatic?
answer: By adjusting a control program or by defining an active power flow over a virtual tie-line between the LFC areas (Article 147(4)(b)); adjusting the active power flows over HVDC interconnectors is the third option (Article 147(4)(c)).
review_note: reworded after the first Sonnet pass (see docs/qa_eu_hard_review.md)

q: May a netting arrangement that offsets simultaneous opposite reserve activations between control areas move more power than the area would itself need to activate to bring its control error to zero?
answer: No: the imbalance netting power interchange of an LFC area must not exceed the actual amount of FRR activation necessary to regulate the FRCE of that LFC area to zero without imbalance netting power interchange (Article 146(6)).

q: Which method for allocating cross-border capacity to the exchange of reserves is meant for contracts longer than one day that are concluded more than a week before delivery?
answer: The allocation process based on an economic efficiency analysis: it applies where the contracting period is more than one day and the contracting is done more than one week in advance of the provision of the balancing capacity (Article 42(1)).

q: Which of the cross-border capacity allocation approaches for reserves has the TSOs allocate capacity to energy bids and to reserve bids in a single optimisation, covering both implicit and explicit auctions?
answer: The co-optimised allocation process: its methodology contains “a detailed description of how cross-zonal capacity shall be allocated to bids for the exchange of energy and bids for the exchange of balancing capacity or sharing of reserves in a single optimisation process performed for both implicit and explicit auctions” (Article 40(1)(b)).

q: When cross-border capacity is set aside for sharing reserves (not for exchanging them) under the co-optimised or market-based approaches, how is its actual market value determined?
answer: It is calculated based on the avoided costs of procuring balancing capacity (Article 39(4)); for the exchange of balancing capacity it is based on the balancing capacity bids submitted to the capacity procurement optimisation function (Article 39(3)).

q: If cross-border capacity was set aside for exchanging reserve capacity but turned out not to be used for the associated energy exchange, what can it be released for?
answer: For the exchange of balancing energy with shorter activation times or for operating the imbalance netting process (Article 38(9)).

q: When cross-border capacity is still free after the last intraday cross-zonal gate closure, what may transmission operators use it for?
answer: They shall use it for the exchange of balancing energy or for the operation of the imbalance netting process (Article 17(3)).

q: May cross-border capacity on a direct-current interconnector be allocated to the exchange of frequency containment reserves, even though the reliability margin normally serves that purpose?
answer: Yes: the reliability margin is used for operating and exchanging frequency containment reserves, “except on Direct Current (‘DC’) interconnectors for which cross-zonal capacity for operating and exchanging frequency containment reserves may also be allocated” (Article 38(4)).

q: Day-ahead or intraday cross-border capacity sold in an explicit auction is cut because the TSO invokes an emergency, not force majeure. What compensation are the holders entitled to?
answer: Compensation equal to the price difference of the relevant markets between the bidding zones concerned in the relevant time-frame (Article 72(3)(c)); if the bidding zone price is not calculated in at least one of the two zones, reimbursement of the price paid for the capacity (Article 72(3)(d)).
review_note: reworded after the first Sonnet pass (see docs/qa_eu_hard_review.md)

q: A TSO has to cut back long-term cross-border capacity that is already allocated. Whom does it ask to launch the coordinated calculation of the necessary curtailments, and what must it supply with the request?
answer: It sends a request to the responsible coordinated capacity calculator, supported with all relevant information (Article 25(2)).

q: What must the method for dividing cross-border congestion revenue provide for when the interconnecting assets belong to someone other than a TSO?
answer: It must establish arrangements to share congestion income deriving from transmission assets owned by parties other than TSOs (Article 73(2)(e)).

q: By what date did TSOs have to hand ACER the method governing how revenue from scarce cross-border capacity may be spent, and how long did ACER have to decide on it?
answer: By 5 July 2020; ACER had to decide on the proposed methodology within six months of receiving it (Article 19(4)).

q: Besides an emergency and the impossibility of redispatching or countertrading, what further condition must be met before a TSO may cut capacity already allocated on an interconnector as one of its grid-security countermeasures?
answer: That all TSOs at the given interconnector agree to such adjustment; the curtailment is also limited to an emergency situation where using that capacity endangers operational security and where re-dispatching or countertrading is not possible (Article 22(1)(i)).
review_note: reworded after the first Sonnet pass (see docs/qa_eu_hard_review.md)

q: If voltage deterioration threatens to cause a voltage collapse, may a transmission operator tell the distribution grids and large users connected to it to switch off the automatic regulation of their transformers?
answer: Yes: the remedial action in Article 22(1)(c)(iv) is “instructing transmission-connected DSOs and significant grid users to block automatic voltage and reactive power control of transformers or to activate on their facilities the remedial actions set out in points (i) to (iii)”.

q: May a grid operator use security measures beyond the standard list of corrective actions, and what reporting follows?
answer: Yes, where necessary and justified to maintain operational security; the TSO must report and justify those instances to the regulatory authority and, where applicable, the Member State, at least once a year after activation, and the reports and justifications are published (Article 22(2)).

q: When a transmission operator activates a security measure, are the affected distribution operators and large grid users obliged to carry out its instructions?
answer: Yes: when a TSO activates a remedial action, each impacted transmission-connected significant grid user and DSO shall execute the instructions given by the TSO (Article 23(4)).

q: When cross-border capacity is calculated, must corrective measures that cost nothing to apply be reflected in the calculation?
answer: Yes: each TSO shall take into account remedial actions without costs in capacity calculation (Article 25(5)).

q: For battery storage owned by a distribution grid operator, up to which date must the final investment decision have been taken for the battery to keep running for its usual depreciation period despite the phase-out rule?
answer: Until 4 July 2019, provided the battery is connected to the grid within two years, integrated into the distribution system, used only for the reactive instantaneous restoration of network security and not used to buy or sell electricity on electricity markets (Article 36(4)).

q: In a derogation from the ban on a transmission operator holding energy storage, is the need to supply non-frequency ancillary services an accepted ground?
answer: Yes: the conditions in Article 54(2)(b) are that “such facilities or non-frequency ancillary services are necessary for the transmission system operators to fulfil their obligations” for the efficient, reliable and secure operation of the transmission system and that they are not used to buy or sell electricity in the electricity markets; the tendering and regulatory-assessment conditions in points (a) and (c) must also be fulfilled.
review_note: reworded after the first Sonnet pass (see docs/qa_eu_hard_review.md)

q: Which type of system operator is made responsible, in the list of its tasks, for data management systems including cybersecurity?
answer: Transmission system operators: “data management, including the development of data management systems, cybersecurity and data protection, subject to the applicable rules” is one of their responsibilities (Article 40(1)(m)).
review_note: reworded after the first Sonnet pass (see docs/qa_eu_hard_review.md)

q: Which grid operator must act as a neutral market facilitator when buying the energy it uses to cover losses in its system?
answer: The distribution system operator, where it has such a function, in accordance with transparent, non-discriminatory and market-based procedures (Article 31(5)).

q: Must a distribution grid operator buy voltage-support type services (non-frequency ancillary services) through market-based procedures, and what exempts it?
answer: Yes, through transparent, non-discriminatory and market-based procedures, unless the regulatory authority has assessed that market-based provision is economically not efficient and has granted a derogation; the obligation does not apply to fully integrated network components (Article 31(7)).

q: For renewable plants commissioned from 2026, below what size can Member States exempt them from paying for the imbalances they cause?
answer: Below 200 kW: for power-generating facilities commissioned from 1 January 2026, the small-renewables derogation of Article 5(2)(b) (400 kW until then) applies only to installations of less than 200 kW (Article 5(4)).
review_note: reworded after the first Sonnet pass (see docs/qa_eu_hard_review.md)

q: For renewable plants commissioned from the start of 2026, what is the upper size limit for getting priority when system operators dispatch generation?
answer: Less than 200 kW: from 1 January 2026 the priority dispatch of Article 12(2)(a) (400 kW until then) applies only to power-generating facilities using renewable energy sources with an installed electricity capacity of less than 200 kW (Article 12(5)).

q: When does a renewable plant commissioned before 4 July 2019 that was entitled to dispatch priority lose that priority?
answer: From the date on which the power-generating facility becomes subject to significant modifications, deemed at least where a new connection agreement is required or where its generation capacity is increased (Article 12(6)).

q: Up to what plant size may Member States give priority dispatch to electricity from high-efficiency cogeneration?
answer: To facilities with an installed electricity capacity of less than 400 kW (Article 12(4)).

q: Until what point may a party responsible for balance freely change the schedules used to calculate its position?
answer: Prior to the intraday cross-zonal gate closure time (Article 17(3)); after it only the internal commercial schedules may be changed, under the rules of the terms and conditions related to balancing (Article 17(4)).

q: In a system where the operator itself dispatches plants, how many positions may a balance responsible party hold per imbalance area?
answer: Several final positions per imbalance area, equal to the generation schedules of power generating facilities or the consumption schedules of demand facilities, until the harmonisation proposal of Article 52(2) is implemented (Article 54(3)(c)).

q: If balancing energy was activated, what ceiling applies to the price paid to a party whose imbalance is a surplus?
answer: The imbalance price for positive imbalance shall not be greater than the weighted average price for negative activated balancing energy from frequency restoration reserves and replacement reserves; if there was no activation, the value of the avoided activation of such balancing energy (Article 55(5)).

q: Until when could regulators grant derogations from the 15-minute imbalance settlement period, and what limit applies from January 2025?
answer: Derogations may be granted only until 31 December 2024; from 1 January 2025 the settlement period shall not exceed 30 minutes where an exemption has been granted by all the regulatory authorities within a synchronous area (Article 8(4)).

q: May a TSO deal directly with another country's providers to exchange balancing energy from restoration reserves without doing the same for the reserve capacity behind it?
answer: No: the TSO-BSP model for the exchange of balancing energy from frequency restoration reserves may be applied only where the TSO-BSP model is also applied for the exchange of balancing capacity for frequency restoration reserves (Article 35(5)); replacement reserves have a wider rule (Article 35(6)).

q: Counted from the decision to launch a review of existing price zone layouts, how long do the participating TSOs have to submit a joint proposal to maintain or amend the layout?
answer: Within 15 months of the decision to launch a review (Article 32(4)(b)(iii)).

q: How long after the regulators approve the methodology and assumptions of a price zone review must the participating TSOs submit their joint proposal to amend or maintain the zone configuration?
answer: No later than 12 months after approval of the methodology and assumptions (Article 14(6)).

q: Under what conditions can a single TSO start a review of price zone borders inside its own control area on its own?
answer: Yes, one single regulatory authority or TSO, with the approval of its competent regulatory authority, may launch a review for the bidding zones inside the TSO's control area if the configuration has negligible impact on neighbouring TSOs' control areas and the review is necessary to improve efficiency or maintain operational security (Article 32(1)(d)); the TSO is then the only participating TSO (Article 32(3)).
review_note: reworded after the first Sonnet pass (see docs/qa_eu_hard_review.md)

q: How is the imbalance of a balance responsible party defined as an energy volume?
answer: An energy volume calculated for a balance responsible party that represents the difference between the allocated volume attributed to it and its final position, including any imbalance adjustment, within a given imbalance settlement period (Article 2(8)).
review_note: reworded after the first Sonnet pass (see docs/qa_eu_hard_review.md)

q: How is a party that can supply reserves to grid operators described in terms of the equipment it controls?
answer: A market participant with reserve-providing units or reserve-providing groups able to provide balancing services to TSOs (Article 2(6)).
